lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the US-China tech war
lead.head: Chips off the old bloc
body: Ajay Shah’s most amazing purchase of the years before 1991 was an early chess computer. You moved the pieces, an LED blinked, and it told you its move. A neighbour flying to Singapore had brought it back. Amit Varma had the same one.

You would think such hunting was a distant memory, Shah said. Instead it is back, in Shanghai and in Kazakhstan, and this time the prize is chips. “You are now back to a black market for microchips,” he said. {064-S01}
The culprit this time is not Indian protectionism but American export controls aimed at China, the subject of the episode: what the hosts call the global tech wars.
## From friends to foes

Until about 2016, Varma said, Democrats and Republicans agreed that free trade was good and that America should engage with China. Doubts began inside the Obama administration. Donald Trump won with simple narratives that were wrong but easy to grasp. Joe Biden promised to reverse him, then sided with his hawks.
“In just eight years, everything is switched around,” Varma said, “and the consensus now is that we are at war with China.” {064-C01}
The war, he said, stands on a three-legged stool: industrial policy, tariffs and export controls.

The controls are the sharpest leg. Shah said the only comparable precedent is the West’s blockade of the USSR before 1989. Today any company anywhere that uses American tools to do work for a Chinese customer can be sanctioned.
## Why it went to hell

Shah traced the turn to misbehaviour multiplied by size. China, he said, by and large cheated on its WTO promises, and stole intellectual property. India misbehaved on trade too, but India was small. China became systemically important.
Then Russia invaded Ukraine, with weapons built in factories that held German machine tools and Western electronics, and Xi Jinping backed the invasion while rattling sabres over Taiwan.
Shah is sympathetic to the response. “It is better to do economic warfare than to do real warfare,” he said. {064-C07}

Varma is not. A selective globalisation, he argued, is no more globalisation than crony capitalism is capitalism, and economic warfare hurts ordinary people on both sides. “To me economic warfare is economic warfare,” he said, “and I’m fundamentally against economic warfare at all times.” {064-C08}
## What comes next

Export controls helped the West win the Cold War, Shah said, but a determined country can string many cheap chips together in parallel. Against a fixed target such as a nuclear bomb, the bans only add delay and pain.

Where they can bite is in races: the drone war over Ukraine, artillery, winner-takes-all markets. “You don’t need to indefinitely be better,” Shah said. “You only need to be a little bit better.” {064-C12}
Whether it will work against China, he stressed, the jury is still out.

Varma warned of reflexivity. Squeezing China could make it more desperate over Taiwan, and its push into legacy chips could sink rivals, India’s chip ambitions included. “All of this rationale sounds great,” he said, “but unintended consequences will compound.”
Shah agreed that there would be surprises. When the hosts reconvene on the subject in a year, he said, “we’ll get caught by surprise”.

Their reading lists ended the episode on China itself. Varma recommended two books by Yuen Yuen Ang, rejecting a “good versus evil” view of a deeply complex country. Shah chose an interview with Michael Pettis, calling it “absolutely eye opening”.

second.label: America and China
second.head: A mission, not a deal
second.deck: Ajay Shah says US engagement with China was idealism, not just realpolitik
body: American engagement with China was never only about interests and realpolitik, Ajay Shah said. It was idealism, of a kind Indians find hard to picture, and he has seen it face to face. {064-C04}

After Richard Nixon re-established economic relations in 1972 and Deng Xiaoping came to power in 1978, American society and the state signed on to “the China project”. After the USSR collapsed in 1989, the mood was that 2,000 years of fighting between Persia and Athens had ended, and Athens had won. {064-J06}

China, the thinking went, would wise up into a free-market liberal democracy, given time. So the West gave it access to science, technology and trade, and Bill Clinton championed its entry into the WTO.

quote.text: All through the twentieth century there has been a sense in America that China is our responsibility

second.caption: America’s civilising mission

third.head: Deng gets a split verdict
body: Ajay Shah says Deng Xiaoping failed. His dream of turning China into a normal country, Shah argued, fell apart when Xi Jinping concentrated power and China went back to being a communist country. {#dengfailed}
Amit Varma strongly disagrees. Deng, he said, is one of the great men of history. “Hundreds of millions of people out of poverty means hundreds and millions of successes.” {064-C09}

Deng also made a better political outcome more likely than a Mao-like figure would have, Varma argued. Blaming him for Xi, he said, is like saying Nehru failed had Indira Gandhi not called off the Emergency.

Shah held his ground: if Donald Trump won and cancelled democracy, he would say the US Constitution had not delivered the goods. “I can’t disagree more strongly,” Varma replied, “but we’ll move on.” {#disagree}

p2.title: War by other means
p2.deck: How America turned on China, why, and whether it will work, as argued by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: The great drama
sections.head: Eight years, one about-turn
sections.caption: the bipartisan U-turn on China
body: Until recently, Amit Varma said, there was a bipartisan consensus in the US: free trade is a good thing, and America should engage with China. It was almost like the end of history, to use Francis Fukuyama’s “often misinterpreted phrase”. {064-J05}

Around 2016, even before the election, voices inside the Obama administration began to question it, including Jake Sullivan, now the national security adviser. “So it wasn’t as if everything happened with Trump,” Varma said.

Donald Trump, he argued, rose on simple narratives that were wrong but that people could get, especially in a Midwest that had lost jobs: immigrants are taking your job, and your jobs are being shipped overseas.
## Where you sit

Joe Biden said in 2019 that he would reverse Trump’s policies. In office, his team split. Janet Yellen, his treasury secretary, wanted to engage China and lower tariffs. Katherine Tai, his trade chief, wanted them higher, and “perhaps where you stand depends on where you sit”, Varma said. {064-J08}
In the end, Varma said, Biden agreed with Sullivan, and America went in that direction. Now, for the first time, the bipartisan consensus points the opposite way. {064-C01}
~ Varma drew on a piece by Greg Ip in the *Wall Street Journal*, and said the first draft of this history is being written right now.

quote.text: One of the reasons for his success I’ve often speculated is that he came up with these simple narratives which everyone could understand.

sections.label: How it is fought
sections.head: Three legs to stand on
sections.caption: the reach of export controls
body: America’s campaign, Amit Varma said, is a three-legged stool. First comes industrial policy with heavy subsidies: TSMC of Taiwan announced in 2020 a fab in Arizona, and with subsidies is now opening three. {#tsmc}

India tried industrial policy in the fifties and sixties, Varma noted, “and it’s not a good way to think about the world”. The second leg is tariffs, which rose under both Trump and Biden. The third is export controls, to stop the flow of chips and intellectual property. Chips matter because so much science now happens by simulation at scale. {064-C02}
## The long arm

Ajay Shah said the only real analogy is the West’s pre-1989 blockade of the USSR; Japan, Holland and Germany now sing the same tune. ASML’s most advanced chipmaking machines cannot go to China or Russia. Nor can American design software, and all the world’s semiconductor work, he said, runs on three American software systems. {#software}
An Indian firm using those tools to design chips for a Chinese customer would be sanctioned too. {064-C03} American citizens and green-card holders may not work in these sectors in China.

~ Varma singled out the Foreign Direct Product Rule as particularly pernicious. Under it, goods made abroad with American technology or software count as American, even if they never cross the border. {#fdpr} Its first target was Huawei.

quote.text: It is an amazing depth of export controls that is sought to be imposed upon not just China, but the whole world.

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Too big to misbehave
sections.caption: why the West turned on China
body: Ajay Shah began with idealism. America felt it had a civilising mission in China, he said, and hoped it would become a liberal democracy. Under Xi Jinping, he said, that project fell apart. Shah says Deng Xiaoping failed; Amit Varma, who calls Deng one of the great men of history, strongly disagrees.
Then bad behaviour piled up. By and large, China cheated on the promises it made on joining the WTO. There was government-backed theft of software, and cyber attacks by China and Russia.

India, Shah said, has been a prime exponent of misbehaviour on trade too, demanding openness while staying protectionist. But it did not matter: “India is inconsequential.” China became systemically important. {064-C05}
## The war that changed minds
Then Russia invaded Ukraine, a war that, Shah said, could credibly be called funded by European gas purchases. Why, people asked, fight a threat the West had itself enabled?

Xi Jinping doubled down, backing Russia and reserving the right to invade Taiwan. China came to be seen as a revisionist power: one, Shah explained, that questions the international order and seeks to disrupt it by force. {#revisionist}
~ Shah separated three stories that often get mixed up: the third globalisation, the tech war that began in 2022, and a short-term Chinese problem of overproduction. {064-C14}

quote.text: China became big. China became systemically important.

sections.label: The quarrel
sections.head: Better than bullets?
sections.caption: economic warfare
body: Ajay Shah is sympathetic to the West’s reasoning. As an economist he wants world peace and full globalisation, he said, but if the choice is between killing people and interfering with a rogue power’s prosperity, he will take the second. {064-C07}
With a hot war under way, and Xi Jinping never backing away from his claim on Taiwan, he called the tech war a reasonable strategy.

Amit Varma is not convinced. Freedom and voluntary exchange, he argued, should be foundational, not contingent. And who sets the rules America claims to enforce? “Who defines a frickin’ global order?” he asked. {#frickin}
Trade is positive-sum, Varma said. When the Swiss keep zero tariffs on Indian goods while India keeps its own, it is no favour to India: “They’re doing it for their own benefit.”
## Doctors and drones

One answer to China’s drone dominance, Varma said, citing Noah Smith, is to deregulate America’s own industry so that more people make drones there, rather than to impose export restrictions. {064-R08}
The same goes for India. If local doctors are not good enough, whip them into shape through competition rather than banning foreign doctors, “because then the patient will die”.
~ Varma admitted he had no solution to Chinese IP theft or the threat to Taiwan. “You gotta do something,” he said.

quote.text: The third globalisation is no more globalisation than crony capitalism is capitalism.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.head: Two months’ head start
sections.caption: where sanctions bite
body: Export controls are not new, Ajay Shah said. They were part of how the West won the Cold War. Cut off, the USSR tried self-reliance and never caught up: it could not build computers or CPUs, and never got to Unix. {064-C10}
Recreating a vast body of knowledge is hard, he said, and authoritarian regimes crush the tiny 0.01 per cent of geniuses, “the mavericks”, who might have managed it.
Still, a determined country can do a lot with weaker equipment. Parallel computing strings together hundreds of CPUs, and that capability exists in India, China and Russia. {064-C11}
## Races and targets

Against a fixed target such as a nuclear bomb, Shah said, sanctions are useless. In a race, they may matter: a lag of a month or two in drone design could let Ukrainian drones beat Russian and Chinese ones on the battlefield. {064-C12}
Amit Varma warned that the logic sounds great but the real world reacts. Squeezing China could make it more desperate over Taiwan, and China is ramping up legacy chips. {064-C13}
He recalled America funding guerrillas in Afghanistan against the Soviet Union, Osama bin Laden among them. “And look what happened.” {#afghan}
~ Shah agreed that surprises are coming. Most chips inside a drone are simple legacy chips, he added, so China may end up dominating them globally.

quote.text: Instead of 10 super duper powerful modern Nvidia GPUs, you’ll have 1000 weaker GPUs, you will get to the same compute.

side.boxText: As the China model was collapsing, Ajay Shah said, Xi Jinping chose to side with Russia, keep rattling sabres over Taiwan and insist on the right to invade. He gave the West no reassurance that China was not a rogue nation. {#xi}

contQuote.text: Part one, it’s very difficult to recreate a vast body of knowledge and artifacts. Part two, the people who would have done it are the ones that get hurt the most by an authoritarian regime.

stories.caption: how NSE built PRISM
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how NSE did it with cheap chips
stories.head: Beowulf versus Chicago
body: In the early 1990s, the National Stock Exchange was about to start trading equity derivatives. It wanted a risk management system never seen before: one that ran in real time, and covered not just each clearing member but every single participant.

Chicago had the two great derivatives exchanges, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Chicago Board of Trade. NSE sent Ashish Chauhan, now its CEO, and Susan Thomas to study their risk systems and pick one to buy.

They came home unimpressed. Thomas told NSE’s leadership, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna, that the Chicago systems were 1970s technology, “dull, obsolete stuff”. NSE could do better with a Beowulf cluster: many cheap Intel CPUs computing in parallel.

It works, Ajay Shah explained, because one participant’s risk does not depend on another’s. Amit Varma’s calculation can run on one CPU and the producer Nomsita’s on a second. Varma said neither he nor Nomsita understood “that parallel whatever”, but he was happy their power had been multiplied. {064-J03}

NSE’s IT leadership thought it crazy, and real time impossible. “People in the room all came to blows,” Shah said. Ravi Narayan split the difference: he would fund Thomas to build a proof of concept at IGIDR.
The bar was set at 100 calculations a second, beyond what the incumbents thought possible. {#hundred} Built with Shovam Mishra, the system, called PRISM, succeeded.
~ Endlessly reworked, PRISM still runs the risk management of NSE’s derivatives trading today.
stories.why: If a job splits into independent pieces, many cheap processors can match a few elite ones. That is why Shah thinks blocking top-end chips mostly makes a determined country’s work slower and more painful, not impossible. {064-S04}

stories.start: I want to tell a story from the deep past
stories.end: So it's just so amazing that something's come back
stories.caption: the black market for chips
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a black market he thought was history
stories.head: Nudge nudge, wink wink, Nvidia
body: Before 1991, Ajay Shah recalled, modern electronics were exotic in India. Protectionism kept them out, and people relied on elaborate informal chains, some would say a black market, and on friends travelling abroad.

His most amazing purchase was an early chess computer: you moved the pieces, and an LED blinked to show its reply. A neighbour flying to Singapore brought it home. “I had the same one,” Amit Varma said.
You would think that was a distant memory, Shah said. Instead, in Shanghai today you go nudge nudge, wink wink, to find the dealer who has the right Nvidia A100. {064-S01}
~ Kazakhstan has a bigger black market for a wider array of chips, where people fly in from New Delhi carrying a suitcase of chips to sell for a profit. {#kazakh}
stories.why: Trade barriers do not make technology vanish; they push it underground. The world thought it had finished with that kind of protectionism, Shah said, and now export controls aimed at China have brought it back.
stories.postscript: Varma, recalling the previous episode on knowledge lost and regained, called it “the same shit all over again”. {064-R10}

stories.start: I remember uh there was a time in the late 80s
stories.end: but before the nuclear deal, it was much worse
stories.caption: India under export controls
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s own years under export controls
stories.head: No Sun for India
body: Export controls are not a weapon invented for China. In the late 1980s, Ajay Shah recalled, the latest Sun SPARCstation workstations were not licensed for export to India. If you were in India, you could not buy one. {064-S03}
“Now this is a pitifully weak CPU by modern standards,” he said. “But export controls was a thing.”
Until Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush signed the nuclear deal, the footprint of export controls on Indian buyers was extensive. Some remain even now.

~ The Bureau of Industry and Security, Shah said, had been fading into a less consequential agency. It has since been resurrected and amplified, on a scale he never saw even in the Cold War. {#resurrected}
stories.why: India once lived on the wrong side of export controls, and the West’s Cold War blockade of the USSR set the template. What is new, in Shah’s telling, is the sheer scale of today’s campaign.
stories.postscript: At its Cold War peak the agency issued about 100,000 export licences a year, Amit Varma said; in the 1990s, 10,000; now, 40,000. {#forty}

stories.start: And just in case, gentle reader, you're wondering what we are talking about
stories.end: the price reflected the value as it uh were
stories.caption: the seven-year wait
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s one fact about the pre-1991 economy
stories.head: Second-hand, first in line
body: For listeners born after 1991, Amit Varma had one fact to show how bizarre the old closed economy was: a secondhand car cost more than a new one. {064-S02}
The reason was the queue. A new car came with a waiting list of seven years. A used car was available immediately.

“It didn’t matter what the condition was,” Varma said. The price reflected the value, “as it were”. He pointed listeners to an episode of his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen* on the 1991 reforms, with Ajay Shah and Shruti Rajagopalan.
~ He told the story as a warning. With industrial policy, tariffs and protectionism back between the US and China, he said, “it almost feels as if the world is going backwards”. {#backwards}

quote.text: A secondhand car costs more than a new car. Because a new car would have a wait list of seven years.

quiz.q: What did a neighbour flying to Singapore bring back for Ajay Shah before 1991?
quiz.a: An early chess computer whose LED blinked to show the next move.

quiz.q: Why, in pre-1991 India, could a secondhand car cost more than a new one?
quiz.a: A new car had a seven-year waiting list; a used one came immediately.

quiz.q: What are the three legs of America’s stool in the tech war, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Industrial policy with heavy subsidies, rising tariffs, and export controls on chips and IP.

quiz.q: Which old saying about war did Ajay Shah say no longer holds, and why?
quiz.a: That two countries with McDonald’s never go to war; Russia and Ukraine both had them.

quiz.q: What did Susan Thomas propose to NSE instead of buying a Chicago exchange’s risk system?
quiz.a: A Beowulf cluster: many cheap Intel CPUs computing each participant’s risk in parallel.

quiz.q: Against what kind of goal, by Ajay Shah’s account, are export controls useless?
quiz.a: A fixed target like a nuclear bomb; they can matter only in races.
